title: Exploring Fuel Efficiency with mtcars
text:
Fuel Efficiency and Vehicle Weight
The following figure shows the relationship between vehicle weight and fuel efficiency.

plot(
  cars$wt,
  cars$mpg,
  xlab = "Weight (1000 lbs)",
  ylab = "Miles per gallon",
  main = "Fuel Efficiency vs. Vehicle Weight"
)

abline(lm(mpg ~ wt, data = cars), lwd = 2)







Figure 1: Relationship between vehicle weight and fuel efficiency in the mtcars dataset.

title: Exploring Fuel Efficiency with mtcars
text:
Modeling Fuel Efficiency
Finally, I fit a linear regression model to examine how vehicle weight and horsepower are associated with fuel efficiency.

model <- lm(mpg ~ wt + hp, data = cars)
summary(model)

title: Exploring Fuel Efficiency with mtcars
text:
Findings
The results suggest that heavier cars tend to have lower fuel efficiency. In the regression model, vehicle weight has an estimated coefficient of -3.88, meaning that higher weight is associated with lower miles per gallon when horsepower is held constant. Horsepower also has a negative estimated association with fuel efficiency.
The model has an R-squared value of approximately 0.83, indicating that vehicle weight and horsepower together explain about 83% of the variation in miles per gallon among the cars in this dataset. These results describe associations in the mtcars data and should not be interpreted as evidence of causation.

title: My first weeks in MDS
text:
My first weeks at UBC began before the MDS program officially started. We arrived early to become familiar with the campus and our new surroundings. This gave me some time to settle in and prepare for the journey ahead.
One of the highlights of this period was attending the Mastercard Foundation Scholars Program orientation. It was an exciting opportunity to meet new people, connect with other scholars, and learn more about the community and opportunities available to us.
As the MDS program began on August 31, I was excited to meet my new classmates and learn more about the program. Starting a new academic journey came with both excitement and challenges, but these first experiences helped me feel more connected to UBC and prepared for the intensive months ahead.

title: Iris Flower Analysis
text:
Sepal Length by Species

df["species"] = df["target"].map(dict(enumerate(iris.target_names)))

df.boxplot(column="sepal length (cm)", by="species")
plt.suptitle("")
plt.title("Sepal Length by Iris Species")
plt.xlabel("Species")
plt.ylabel("Sepal Length (cm)")
plt.show()







Figure 1: Sepal length distribution for the three Iris species






Interpretation
The boxplot shows clear differences in sepal length among the three Iris species. Setosa generally has the shortest sepal lengths, virginica has the longest, and versicolor falls between the two. There is some overlap between the distributions, particularly between versicolor and virginica.

title: Iris Flower Analysis
text:
Petal Length vs Petal Width

df.plot.scatter(
    x="petal length (cm)",
    y="petal width (cm)",
    c="target",
    colormap="viridis"
)
plt.title("Petal Length vs Petal Width")
plt.show()









Interpretation
The scatter plot shows a strong positive relationship between petal length and petal width. The three Iris species also form distinct clusters, suggesting that petal measurements are useful for distinguishing between species.

title: About
text:
I have a bachelor’s degree in Computer Science and Engineeringfrom Mekelle Institute of Technology, Ethiopia. Through my studies and previous experiences, I developed a strong foundation in data analytics, AI/ML model development, and programming using Python, R, and SQL.
I am deeply passionate about transforming complex data into actionable insights and developing data-driven solutions that support better decision-making and build stronger communities.
Beyond my technical work, I have volunteer experience in national and international community development. I am also passionate about sustainability, women’s empowerment, and creating opportunities for underserved communities.
As the Founder of the Data for Change initiative and a Sustainability Ambassador at the University of British Columbia, I am committed to connecting data-driven innovation with social and environmental impact.
I strongly believe that data and AI are most powerful when they are used to empower people and create positive change.
My goal is to continue bridging data insights and social impact by modeling data-driven solutions that contribute to a more inclusive, sustainable, and equitable future.
